explanations.answer: The one who cares for the poor
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The very first word of the psalm is "Blessed," and it lands on "…the one who cares for the poor…" (Psalm 41:1). David, Israel's king, doesn't start with a big title or a fancy résumé. He starts with somebody who looks out for people who have little.

explanations.answer: The one who gives at the temple
explanations.explanation: Good guess, because giving at the temple sounds so respectable. But look at what David actually says: "Blessed is the one who cares for the poor…" (Psalm 41:1). The blessing goes to the person looking after those in need. The psalm doesn't mention the temple at all.

explanations.answer: The one who keeps every feast
explanations.explanation: Feasts sound so respectable, so I get why this one tempts you. Still, this psalm doesn't mention them. David opens with "Blessed is the one who cares for the poor…" (Psalm 41:1). The blessing lands on someone who looks after people in need.
Yes, "deliver." David says the LORD "…will deliver him in the day of trouble." (Psalm 41:1). Trouble shows up for everybody, but this person doesn't face it alone. That's good news on a hard day.

I can see why "test" sounds like something that happens on a hard day. But David says the LORD "…will deliver him in the day of trouble." (Psalm 41:1). The word is deliver, which means the LORD brings him through it.

A warning would be nice, like a smoke alarm. But that's not the word David picked. He says the LORD "…will deliver him in the day of trouble." (Psalm 41:1). Deliver means the LORD brings him through it.

Not quite, friend, and this one flips the verse around. David says the LORD will "…refuse to give him over to the will of his foes." (Psalm 41:2). So the answer is False. The LORD does not hand this person over to his enemies.

You got it, baker. The text says the LORD will "…refuse to give him over to the will of his foes." (Psalm 41:2). He's protected, preserved and blessed, and he's not handed over. Enemies don't get the final word here.

Right on the money. David says the LORD "…will sustain him on his bed of illness and restore him from his bed of sickness." (Psalm 41:3). Sustain and restore, those are the two things he does. I think that's a comfort to anybody who's ever been laid up.

A prophet at the bedside would be quite a visitor. But the psalm doesn't mention one. David says the LORD Himself "…will sustain him on his bed of illness and restore him from his bed of sickness." (Psalm 41:3).

Peaceful sleep sounds lovely when you're sick. But that's not what the verse says. David says the LORD "…will sustain him on his bed of illness and restore him from his bed of sickness." (Psalm 41:3). He sustains and he restores.
That's it. David prays, "O LORD, be gracious to me; heal me…" (Psalm 41:4). He takes his sickness straight to the LORD. No hiding it, no fancy speech.
A prayer for a son sounds like a big one, but that's not what David asks here. He prays, "O LORD, be gracious to me; heal me…" (Psalm 41:4). His ask is healing.
Heading home sounds nice, but that's not David's request here. He prays, "O LORD, be gracious to me; heal me…" (Psalm 41:4). The ask is healing, plain and simple.
Yes, and that takes honesty. David prays, "heal me, for I have sinned against You." (Psalm 41:4). He doesn't dress it up. He just says it to the LORD.
It's actually True, friend. Right there in his prayer David says, "heal me, for I have sinned against You." (Psalm 41:4). He tells the LORD plainly.

explanations.answer: When will he die and be forgotten
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. His enemies say it with malice: "When will he die and be forgotten?" (Psalm 41:5). They aren't just wishing him gone. They want his name gone too, and that's a cold thing to say about a man in a sickbed.

explanations.answer: When will he leave this land for good
explanations.explanation: That's a rough line, but it's not the one in the psalm. His enemies say, "When will he die and be forgotten?" (Psalm 41:5). They're hoping he dies, and that nobody remembers him afterward.

explanations.answer: Who will take his place on the throne
explanations.explanation: The throne is a reasonable guess for a king. But that's not what they say. The psalm says, "When will he die and be forgotten?" (Psalm 41:5). It's about David himself, and about him being forgotten.
That's the word. The visitor "…gathers slander in his heart; he goes out and spreads it abroad." (Psalm 41:6). He takes it out the door and passes it around. Some visitors should come with a receipt.
Wouldn't that be nice? But the verse says the visitor "…speaks falsehood; he gathers slander in his heart; he goes out and spreads it abroad." (Psalm 41:6). What he spreads is slander, not praise.
Hope would've been a lovely thing to carry out of that room. But the psalm says this visitor "…gathers slander in his heart; he goes out and spreads it abroad." (Psalm 41:6). He spreads slander.

Yes, and it's a heavy one. They whisper that "A vile disease has been poured into him; he will never get up from where he lies!" (Psalm 41:8). Verse 7 says they "…imagine the worst for me…" I think that's hard to hear about yourself.

It's actually True, friend. The people who hate David "…imagine the worst for me…" and they whisper, "A vile disease has been poured into him; he will never get up from where he lies!" (Psalm 41:7-8). It's a heavy part, and David doesn't leave it out.

That's the one. David says, "Even my close friend whom I trusted, the one who shared my bread, has lifted up his heel against me." (Psalm 41:9). Enemies are one thing. A friend from your own table hits different.

A stranger would hurt less, wouldn't it? But David says it's "…my close friend whom I trusted, the one who shared my bread…" (Psalm 41:9). Gath doesn't come into it. This one came from inside his circle.

Close, since it's someone near him. But David doesn't say servant. He says, "…my close friend whom I trusted, the one who shared my bread, has lifted up his heel against me." (Psalm 41:9). A friend he trusted.

explanations.answer: Be gracious and raise him up
explanations.explanation: That's his ask. David prays, "But You, O LORD, be gracious to me and raise me up…" (Psalm 41:10). He turns to the LORD for it, which is where he went back in verse 4 too.

explanations.answer: Send him far away from them
explanations.explanation: Running sounds tempting with a crowd whispering. But David doesn't ask for that. He prays, "But You, O LORD, be gracious to me and raise me up…" (Psalm 41:10).

explanations.answer: Let him hide until it passes
explanations.explanation: Hiding is a very human idea when a crowd is whispering. But David doesn't ask for it. He prays, "But You, O LORD, be gracious to me and raise me up…" (Psalm 41:10). His ask is to be raised up.

Not quite. David doesn't say his enemies stopped whispering. He says, "By this I know that You delight in me, for my enemy does not triumph over me." (Psalm 41:11). The sign is that his enemy doesn't win, so the answer is False.

You got it, baker. David's reason is this: "By this I know that You delight in me, for my enemy does not triumph over me." (Psalm 41:11). The text doesn't say the whispering stopped. It says the enemy doesn't triumph.
That's the answer. David says, "…You uphold me and set me in Your presence forever." (Psalm 41:12). His enemies wanted him forgotten. Instead he's set right in front of the LORD, for good.

explanations.answer: On his throne for many years
explanations.explanation: A throne would suit a king, but that's not what David says. He says to the LORD, "In my integrity You uphold me and set me in Your presence forever." (Psalm 41:12). Forever beats "many years" by a mile.

After that friend lifted his heel against him, I think David wouldn't be rushing back to that crowd. And that's not what he says anyway. He says to the LORD, "In my integrity You uphold me and set me in Your presence forever." (Psalm 41:12).

Yes, the LORD. The psalm closes with "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting. Amen and Amen." (Psalm 41:13). It started by blessing a person and ends by blessing the LORD. Nice bookends.
David is a king, so I see the pull. But the psalm ends, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting. Amen and Amen." (Psalm 41:13). The last blessing goes to the LORD.

Priests are a fair guess for a psalm with a heading like this one. But the closing line says, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting. Amen and Amen." (Psalm 41:13). The blessing goes to the LORD.
